summaries.example: Imagine a white wall under yellow lights. The wall may look yellow even though it is still white. Now imagine a dream or hallucination that feels just like seeing a snowy yard, even though no yard is there. These cases make us ask what seeing really is.
summaries.summary: The problem of perception asks how ordinary seeing can put us directly in touch with the world if illusions and hallucinations are possible. In ordinary life, we usually think that we see familiar objects themselves: a tree, a wall, or snow. We also think the way an object appears is partly shaped by that object. Yet a white wall can look yellow in strange light, and a person could have an experience that seems exactly like seeing a snowy yard even when no yard is present. Philosophers use these cases to question whether real seeing, illusion, and hallucination have the same basic nature. Some theories say experience involves special sense-data or particular ways of sensing. Another theory says experience represents the world as being a certain way. Naive realist disjunctivism says genuine perception directly involves ordinary objects, while a matching hallucination is a different kind of event. The debate is not simply about whether we see the world, but about what seeing is.
key_ideas: Our everyday view says that seeing puts us in direct contact with ordinary things, such as walls, snow, and trees.
Illusions and hallucinations seem possible, so our experiences can sometimes lead us away from how things really are.
Some philosophers think all these experiences share one basic kind; others think a real perception and a hallucination are fundamentally different.
The main theories disagree about whether experience involves special inner objects, ways of sensing, representations, or a direct relation to the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Perception is one of our main ways of learning about the world. Understanding it helps us think carefully about mistakes, dreams, appearances, and knowledge. The debate also shows how philosophers examine an ordinary idea—“I see that thing”—when unusual cases make the idea harder to explain.

important_terms.definition: What an experience feels like from the inside, such as how a color or scene appears to you.
The idea that we can perceive ordinary things in the world directly, rather than only noticing something inside our minds.
A mistake in seeing, such as a white wall looking yellow because of unusual light.
An experience that seems like seeing something, even though the thing is not there to be seen.
The idea that seeing, in a good case, puts an ordinary object before your mind in a special way.

questions_to_think_about: If a white wall looks yellow, are you seeing the wall, something else, or both?
Could an experience feel exactly like seeing a tree when there is no tree?
Does a dream show that feelings alone cannot tell us what is really there?
Which seems more important for seeing: what is in the world or what happens in your mind?

summaries.example: Suppose a white wall is viewed in unusual lighting and appears yellow. In the veridical case, the wall appears as it is; in the illusion, the wall is still the object perceived but appears with a quality it lacks. Now compare a possible hallucination that is introspectively indistinguishable from seeing that wall, although no wall is presented. The two cases may feel alike while differing in their relation to the world.
summaries.summary: The Problem of Perception begins with a tension within ordinary perceptual thought. Perceptual experience seems to be an immediate openness to mind-independent objects, and its phenomenal character seems partly determined by those objects and the manner in which they are presented. This supports a form of direct realism. At the same time, illusions show that an object can appear to have a quality it lacks, while hallucinations are possible experiences that are subjectively indistinguishable from veridical perception despite the absence of the relevant object. The argument from illusion and the argument from hallucination attempt to generalize from these problematic cases to all perception, challenging direct presentation of ordinary objects. The theories discussed respond differently. Sense-datum theory posits non-ordinary objects of experience. Adverbialism analyzes experience as being modified in certain ways, such as sensing whitely. Intentionalism treats perception as a form of world-directed representation and can combine this with a causal account of direct perception. Naive realist disjunctivism maintains that veridical perception is constituted partly by a relation to ordinary objects, while denying that a matching hallucination has the same fundamental nature. The debate therefore concerns not merely whether perception reaches the world, but what kind of relation or structure makes that possible.
key_ideas: The ordinary conception combines ordinary objects, direct presentation, a world-involving explanation of phenomenal character, and often the Common Kind Claim.
The argument from illusion uses a difference between how an object appears and how it is; the argument from hallucination uses the possibility of experience without a presented object.
Sense-datum theory preserves presentation but replaces ordinary objects with non-ordinary sense-data; adverbialism explains experience through modified ways of sensing.
Intentionalism explains experience through perceptual representation and may preserve direct realism through an appropriate causal relation to the represented object.

Naive realist disjunctivism rejects the Common Kind Claim: a veridical perception and a matching hallucination can be subjectively indistinguishable without being fundamentally the same kind of event.
A central dispute is whether phenomenology requires a genuine relation to objects, a representational content, or a more basic explanation of experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue connects everyday appearance with deep questions about consciousness, knowledge, and reality. It asks whether the felt character of experience can be explained by objects in the world, by mental representation, or by features of experience itself. It also illustrates a general philosophical method: test a familiar concept against illusions, hallucinations, and other cases where ordinary assumptions pull apart.

important_terms.definition: The felt or experiential aspect of a mental event: what undergoing it is like for the subject.
A view according to which perceptual experience directly connects us with ordinary, mind-independent objects.
The proposed perceptual relation in which an object is made present to experience and helps determine its character.
An experience in which an ordinary object is perceived but appears to have a quality it does not actually possess.
An experience subjectively indistinguishable from veridical perception but lacking the relevant presented ordinary object.
The claim that veridical, illusory, and hallucinatory experiences of the same apparent scene share one fundamental kind.
The view that perceptual experience is fundamentally a mental representation of the world, rather than a relation to an intermediary object.
A view holding that genuine perception directly involves ordinary objects, while matching hallucination is a fundamentally different case.

questions_to_think_about: Does subjective indistinguishability support the Common Kind Claim, or only show that introspection cannot tell cases apart?
In the argument from illusion, does the fact that something appears yellow require a directly presented yellow thing?
Can intentional representation explain phenomenal character without adding non-intentional qualia?
If a hallucination and a perception have the same proximate brain cause, must they be experiences of the same fundamental kind?
Which theory best preserves the ordinary sense that perception opens us onto a mind-independent world?

summaries.example: A white shirt can look greenish under colored lights. You are still looking at the shirt, but it appears to have a color it does not really have. A different case would be a perfectly convincing hallucination of the shirt when no shirt is present. Both experiences might feel the same from the inside, which raises a puzzle about what they have in common.
summaries.summary: The Problem of Perception examines a conflict between common sense and unusual cases. In everyday perception, we seem to encounter ordinary objects directly. A tree, a wall, or a snowy yard appears to be present to us, and the object seems to help determine how the experience feels. This is the basic idea behind direct realism. But perception can go wrong. An illusion involves a real object that looks unlike its actual properties. A hallucination can seem just like a successful perception even though the relevant object is absent. Philosophers ask whether these experiences share one fundamental kind. The argument from illusion and the argument from hallucination use that possibility to challenge direct presentation of ordinary objects. Different theories respond in different ways. Sense-datum theory introduces non-ordinary objects that are directly experienced. Adverbialism says that experience is modified in ways such as sensing “whitely,” without requiring experienced objects. Intentionalism says that perception represents the world and may still count as direct perception when the representation is appropriately caused by the object. Naive realist disjunctivism says a genuine perception is directly related to ordinary objects, while a matching hallucination is fundamentally different, even if the person cannot tell the difference. The entry presents these views as competing attempts to explain both the success and the possibility of error in perception.
key_ideas: Our normal way of thinking treats perception as being about ordinary objects, not merely private inner pictures.
Illusion and hallucination create pressure because they can seem similar to successful perception while differing in what is actually present.
The argument from illusion says that if an experience needs something with the appearance-quality, perhaps we are not directly seeing the ordinary object.
The argument from hallucination says that if a hallucination can feel exactly like a real perception, perhaps both experiences have the same basic structure.
Sense-datum theory, adverbialism, intentionalism, and naive realist disjunctivism offer different solutions.
The disagreement concerns whether perception is a relation, a way of sensing, a representation, or different things in different cases.
summaries.why_it_matters: We rely on perception in ordinary action and in forming beliefs about the world. The problem shows why perceptual error does not merely create a small practical inconvenience: it raises questions about consciousness, reality, and how experience gives us reasons to believe things. Comparing the theories also helps us see how one unusual case can challenge a whole picture of the mind.

important_terms.definition: The way an experience feels to the person having it, including how colors, shapes, or scenes seem.
The view that perception gives us direct contact with ordinary objects that exist independently of being perceived.
A special perceptual connection in which an object is made present to the mind and helps shape the experience.
A perceptual mistake in which a real object appears different from the way it is.
An experience that seems like a perception but occurs without the relevant ordinary object being there.
The claim that real perceptions, illusions, and hallucinations can belong to one basic kind of experience.
The view that perception represents the world as being a certain way; it need not involve a special inner object.
The view that real perception and matching hallucination are fundamentally different kinds of experience.

questions_to_think_about: Can an object be directly perceived even when it looks different from how it really is?
Is feeling the same from the inside enough to show that two experiences have the same nature?
Does a mental representation need a real object behind it?
Why might someone prefer a theory that keeps direct contact with ordinary objects?
What would count as a good explanation of why an experience has its particular feel?
